speaker: Unknown
en: Are you passionate about software development and the tech industry?
zh: 你对软件开发和科技行业充满热情吗?

speaker: Unknown
en: Software Engineering Daily is looking for a new podcast host to grow its hosting team.
zh: Software Engineering Daily 正在寻找一位新的播客主持人来扩充其主持团队。

speaker: Unknown
en: In this role, you'll help shape the show's editorial direction and interview engineers, founders, hackers, and tech leaders.
zh: 在这个职位上,你将帮助塑造节目的编辑方向,并采访工程师、创始人、黑客和科技领袖。

speaker: Unknown
en: Podcasting experience is a plus, but not required.
zh: 有播客经验是加分项,但不是必需的。

speaker: Unknown
en: Curiosity, great communication skills, and a genuine interest in the craft of building software are what matter most.
zh: 最重要的是好奇心、出色的沟通能力,以及对构建软件这门手艺的真正兴趣。

speaker: Unknown
en: If this sounds like you, reach out at editor at softwareengineeringdaily.com.
zh: 如果这听起来像你,请联系 editor at softwareengineeringdaily.com。

speaker: Unknown
en: Cory Doctorow is a science fiction author, journalist, and technology activist, and a special advisor to the Electronic Frontier Foundation.
zh: Cory Doctorow 是一位科幻作家、记者、科技活动家,也是电子前哨基金会的特别顾问。

speaker: Unknown
en: He is the author of dozens of books, including the nonfiction InShittification, Why Everything Suddenly Got Worse and What to Do About It, and the novel Picks and Shovels.
zh: 他著有数十本书,包括非虚构作品 InShittification、Why Everything Suddenly Got Worse and What to Do About It,以及小说 Picks and Shovels。

speaker: Unknown
en: His work spans tech policy books like The Internet Con and Chokepoint Capitalism, the solar punk novels Walk Away and The Lost Cause,
zh: 他的作品涵盖科技政策书籍如 The Internet Con 和 Chokepoint Capitalism,太阳朋克小说 Walk Away 和 The Lost Cause,

speaker: Unknown
en: And the best-selling YA Little Brother series.
zh: 以及畅销的青少年小说 Little Brother 系列。

speaker: Unknown
en: He holds honorary doctorates from York University and Open University, writes the daily blog Pluralistic.net, and lives in Los Angeles and London.
zh: 他拥有约克大学和开放大学的荣誉博士学位,撰写每日博客 Pluralistic.net,居住在洛杉矶和伦敦。

speaker: Unknown
en: In this episode, Corey joins Josh Goldberg to talk about his latest book, The Reverse Centaur's Guide to Life After AI.
zh: 在本期节目中,Cory 与 Josh Goldberg 一起讨论他的最新著作《The Reverse Centaur's Guide to Life After AI》。

speaker: Unknown
en: They discuss the difference between a centaur and a reverse centaur.
zh: 他们讨论了半人马和反向半人马之间的区别。

speaker: Unknown
en: Why the same AI tools leave some workers empowered and others feeling exploited.
zh: 为什么同样的 AI 工具会让一些员工感到被赋能,而另一些人却感到被剥削。

speaker: Unknown
en: Why companies impose worse performing workflows anyway.
zh: 为什么公司仍然强推表现更差的工作流程。

speaker: Unknown
en: And what workers can do about it.
zh: 以及员工能对此做些什么。

speaker: Unknown
en: This episode is hosted by Josh Goldberg, front-end developer at Sentry and open source maintainer.
zh: 本期节目由 Sentry 前端开发者、开源维护者 Josh Goldberg 主持。

speaker: Unknown
en: Josh works on projects in the TypeScript ecosystem, most notably TypeScript ESLint, a powerful static analysis toolset for JavaScript and TypeScript.
zh: Josh 从事 TypeScript 生态系统的项目工作,最著名的是 TypeScript ESLint,一个用于 JavaScript 和 TypeScript 的强大静态分析工具集。

speaker: Unknown
en: Josh is also the author of the O'Reilly Learning TypeScript book, a Microsoft MVP for developer technologies,
zh: Josh 也是 O'Reilly《Learning TypeScript》一书的作者、微软开发者技术领域的 MVP,

speaker: Unknown
en: And a co-founder of SquiggleConf, a conference for excellent web developer tooling.
zh: 以及 SquiggleConf 的联合创始人,这是一个专注于优秀 Web 开发者工具的会议。

speaker: Unknown
en: Find Josh on Blue Sky, Fostadon, and .com as Joshua K. Goldberg.
zh: 你可以在 Blue Sky、Fostadon 和 .com 上以 Joshua K. Goldberg 找到 Josh。

speaker: Unknown
en: With me today is Cory Doctorow.
zh: 今天和我在一起的是 Cory Doctorow。

speaker: Unknown
en: Cory is a writer, activist, journalist who has been with the Electronic Frontier Foundation, or EFF, for nearly 25 years.
zh: Cory 是一位作家、活动家、记者,在电子前哨基金会(EFF)工作了近 25 年。

speaker: Unknown
en: Cory, welcome to Software Engineering Daily.
zh: Cory,欢迎来到 Software Engineering Daily。

speaker: Unknown
en: Well, thank you for having me on.
zh: 嗯,感谢你们邀请我来。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's a pleasure.
zh: 这是我的荣幸。

speaker: Unknown
en: Well, we're so excited.
zh: 嗯,我们非常兴奋。

speaker: Unknown
en: You got a lot of stuff under your belt.
zh: 你有很多成就。

speaker: Unknown
en: Some people may know you as a sci-fi author or author of very many books on society and tech and culture.
zh: 有些人可能知道你是科幻作家,或者写了很多关于社会、科技和文化的书的作者。

speaker: Unknown
en: Other folks may know you as the insidification guy.
zh: 另一些人可能知道你是「insidification 那个人」。

speaker: Unknown
en: Would you like to start us off by saying how you got into tech and writing?
zh: 你愿意先跟我们讲讲你是怎么进入科技和写作领域的吗?

speaker: Unknown
en: Oh my gosh.
zh: 哦,天哪。

speaker: Unknown
en: Well, I got into tech because my dad was a computer scientist.
zh: 嗯,我进入科技领域是因为我父亲是一名计算机科学家。

speaker: Unknown
en: So our first computer wasn't even electric.
zh: 所以我们的第一台电脑甚至不是电动的。

speaker: Unknown
en: It was mechanical.
zh: 它是机械的。

speaker: Unknown
en: We had a computer called a cardiac.
zh: 我们有一台叫 cardiac 的电脑。

speaker: Unknown
en: A very low powered cardboard Turing complete device that was invented at Bell Labs by engineers who were worried that you had an incoming generation post transistor who wouldn't understand how actual like logic gates worked and who built a cardboard computer that you printed out while they printed it and you assembled and then you move tokens around.
zh: 一个算力非常低的、纸板做的图灵完备装置,由贝尔实验室的工程师发明,他们担心即将到来的后晶体管一代不会理解真正的逻辑门是如何工作的,于是他们造了一台纸板计算机,印出来,你把它组装起来,然后移动代币。

speaker: Unknown
en: You would write out a program and assembler and then it would give you lookup tables.
zh: 你会用汇编写出一个程序,然后它会给你查找表。

speaker: Unknown
en: That would show you how to move the tokens into different registers and the adder and so on to get your output.
zh: 那会告诉你如何把代币移到不同的寄存器和加法器等等里以得到你的输出。

speaker: Unknown
en: So that was in 1976.
zh: 那是在 1976 年。

speaker: Unknown
en: I was five years old.
zh: 我当时五岁。

speaker: Unknown
en: 1977, we got a teletype terminal connected to the University of Toronto via an acoustic coupler.
zh: 1977 年,我们通过一个声学耦合器把一台电传打字机终端连接到了多伦多大学。

speaker: Unknown
en: They had a VAX system there.
zh: 他们那里有一套 VAX 系统。

speaker: Unknown
en: My mom was teaching kindergarten.
zh: 我妈妈在教幼儿园。

speaker: Unknown
en: So, you know, teletype terminal didn't have a screen.
zh: 所以,你知道,电传打字机终端没有屏幕。

speaker: Unknown
en: So you can only compute if you had paper.
zh: 所以只有有纸的时候你才能计算。

speaker: Unknown
en: So she would bring home paper towel from the bathroom.
zh: 所以她会从幼儿园的洗手间带纸巾回家。

speaker: Unknown
en: At kindergarten, we get a thousand feet of computing up one side and a thousand feet down the other side and then roll it back up and send it back to school for the kids to try their hands on.
zh: 在幼儿园,我们在一面算一千英尺,另一面算一千英尺,然后把它卷起来送回学校,让孩子们上手试试。

speaker: Unknown
en: 79, Apple gave all the heads of computer science at all the computer science departments in Ontario Apple II Plus to try for the summer.
zh: 79 年,Apple 给安大略省所有计算机科学系的负责人每人一台 Apple II Plus 试用一个夏天。

speaker: Unknown
en: So my dad was at that point head of computer science at a school in Scarborough outside of Toronto.
zh: 所以我父亲那时是多伦多外士嘉堡一所学校的计算机科学负责人。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so we had an Apple II Plus in 79, 1980, we got a modem.
zh: 所以我们在 79 年、1980 年有了一台 Apple II Plus,我们买了一个调制解调器。

speaker: Unknown
en: We only had enough slots in the machine for either the modem or the 80 column card that gave us lowercase characters.
zh: 机器里的插槽只够插调制解调器或 80 列卡其中之一,80 列卡能让我们显示小写字符。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I don't think I saw a lowercase character for like the next four years because that was where I knew I needed to be.
zh: 我想接下来的大概四年里我都没见过小写字符,因为我知道那才是我需要待的地方。

speaker: Unknown
en: I also at the same time was writing science fiction stories.
zh: 与此同时,我还在写科幻小说。

speaker: Unknown
en: I started selling those as a teenager for a story I saw when I was 17.
zh: 我十几岁时就开始卖那些小说了,我 17 岁时卖出了第一个故事。

speaker: Unknown
en: I ended up dropping out of four undergraduate programs.
zh: 我最后从四个本科项目里退学。

speaker: Unknown
en: Never got a degree, dropped finally out of the University of Waterloo where I was working on what we would today call machine learning.
zh: 从没拿到学位,最后从滑铁卢大学退学,我当时在那里做的是我们今天会称为机器学习的东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: Back then it was cellular automata and took a job programming CD-ROMs for the Voyager company in New York, which was like the coolest multimedia company in the world at the time.
zh: 那时候那是元胞自动机,然后我在纽约的 Voyager 公司找了份给 CD-ROM 编程的工作,那家公司是当时世界上最酷的多媒体公司。

speaker: Unknown
en: When the company kind of imploded, I ended up as a freelance gopher developer.
zh: 当那家公司差不多分崩离析时,我最终成了一名自由职业的 gopher 开发者。

speaker: Unknown
en: And when I finally got my first gopher contract from an ad agency, it was like, we have a client that wants a gopher site.
zh: 当我终于从一家广告公司拿到我的第一个 gopher 合同时,对方说,我们有个客户想要一个 gopher 网站。

speaker: Unknown
en: I wrecked it by coming in and going, you have to see this thing called a web browser.
zh: 我把它搞砸了,我进去就说,你们得看看这个叫网页浏览器的东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so that became a web contract.
zh: 于是那变成了一份 web 合同。

speaker: Unknown
en: I ended up being kind of freelance CIO, worked for a lot of different companies, helping them get on the web and figure out how to wire up their offices and get ISDN modems and did a lot of stuff around the periphery, worked for an executive MBA program on high tech stuff.
zh: 我最终算是成了一名自由职业的 CIO,为很多不同的公司工作,帮他们上网,想办法把办公室连起来,装 ISDN 调制解调器,在外围做了很多事,还为一个高管 MBA 项目做高科技方面的工作。

speaker: Unknown
en: I eventually founded a company with one of my co-founders and a neighbor.
zh: 我最终和一位联合创始人、也是我的邻居创办了一家公司。

speaker: Unknown
en: We raised money in the capital markets.
zh: 我们在资本市场融了钱。

speaker: Unknown
en: During the dot-com bubble, I moved to San Francisco and then ended up working for the Electronic Frontier Foundation, where I worked for the next 25 years, and here I am.
zh: 在互联网泡沫期间,我搬到了旧金山,然后最终去了电子前线基金会工作,在那里工作了接下来的 25 年,然后就到了今天。

speaker: Unknown
en: And here you are.
zh: 然后你就到了这里。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's interesting that we're here to talk about your book about reverse centaurs, AI, machine learning, and you had machine learning on your resume in your life before it was even called machine learning.
zh: 有意思的是,我们今天在这里要聊你那本关于反向半人马、AI、机器学习的书,而你的履历在机器学习还没被叫做机器学习之前就有机器学习了。

speaker: Unknown
en: How does it feel to have witnessed the rise of it from cellular autonomy to AI as an agentic workflows?
zh: 从元胞自动机到作为智能体工作流的 AI,见证它的崛起是什么感受?

speaker: Unknown
en: Oh, well, this isn't the first time that's happened.
zh: 哦,这已经不是第一次发生这种事了。

speaker: Unknown
en: My dad's master's degree in applied mathematics, which is what they called computer science before they called it that at the University of Waterloo, was also cellular automata stuff, except his was on punch cards.
zh: 我爸的应用数学硕士学位——在滑铁卢大学,那是计算机科学还没被这么称呼时的叫法——做的也是元胞自动机的东西,只不过他用的是打孔卡。

speaker: Unknown
en: You know, AI has been through a lot of winters.
zh: 你知道,AI 已经经历过很多次寒冬了。

speaker: Unknown
en: And because we have this phenomenon of buzzword compliance and a highly financialized tech sector, it is normal that whatever is hot gets called that thing.
zh: 而且因为我们有「流行词合规」这种现象,以及一个高度金融化的科技行业,所以 whatever 正在火热的东西就会被叫成那个名字,这很正常。

speaker: Unknown
en: So I have watched the tech sector describe every technology as push, as metaverse, as Web 2.0, as Web 3.0, you know, you name it.
zh: 所以我目睹过科技行业把每项技术都说成是 push、是元宇宙、是 Web 2.0、是 Web 3.0,你随便说。

speaker: Unknown
en: There has been a kind of mania for hastily changing the pitch deck to include the new thing and to the extent that the company has shipped a product that people use to bolt this entirely superfluous add-on to a product that people use often to its great detriment and sometimes to the fatal detriment of the company.
zh: 有一种狂热就是匆忙地改 pitch deck 把新东西加进去,以至于只要公司发布了人们使用的产品,就会把这种完全多余的附加功能硬塞到人们使用的产品上,常常极大地损害产品,有时甚至给公司带来致命的损害。

speaker: Unknown
en: As a fake computer scientist, I never got a CS degree, although I hold an honorary doctorate in computer science from the Open University in the UK, and I'm a visiting professor of CS at the OU.
zh: 作为一个冒牌计算机科学家——我从没拿到计算机科学学位,尽管我拥有英国开放大学的计算机科学荣誉博士学位,而且我还是开放大学的计算机科学客座教授——

speaker: Unknown
en: So as a pretend computer scientist, I look at AI and I say, this is some pretty gnarly and interesting computer science stuff.
zh: 所以作为一个假装的计算机科学家,我看 AI 时会说,这是相当棘手又有趣的计算机科学东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: Fundamentally, what happened was 10 years ago, some scientists said...
zh: 根本上来说,发生的事情是 10 年前,一些科学家说……

speaker: Unknown
en: We have these machine learning algorithms.
zh: 我们有这些机器学习算法。

speaker: Unknown
en: We have an idea for applying a minor variation to the way we operate them.
zh: 我们有一个想法,是对它们运行方式做一个微小的变体。

speaker: Unknown
en: They expected to get a minor variation in the outputs, and instead they got a significant improvement.
zh: 他们预期输出会有一个微小的变体,结果却得到了显著的提升。

speaker: Unknown
en: They found a piece of low-hanging fruit.
zh: 他们找到了一颗低垂的果实。

speaker: Unknown
en: It turned out to be an orchard full of low-hanging fruit.
zh: 结果那是一片满是低垂果实的果园。

speaker: Unknown
en: They could repeat the trick and increase that variation and get a non-linear increase in the outputs.
zh: 他们可以重复这个技巧,增大那个变体,得到输出的非线性增长。

speaker: Unknown
en: But Stein's Law of Finance says anything that can't go on forever eventually stops.
zh: 但斯坦的金融定律说,任何无法永远持续的事情最终都会停止。

speaker: Unknown
en: They reach diminishing returns.
zh: 他们遇到了边际收益递减。

speaker: Unknown
en: And rather than discovering that if you just teach words to the word guessing machine long enough, you eventually create a super intelligence that, if you're unlucky, turns us all into paper clips, they discovered that, as with every other computer science breakthrough, that you are able to achieve some impressive things, and then you've got to think of something else.
zh: 结果他们发现的并不是:只要你教猜词机器猜词教得足够久,你最终就会创造出一个超级智能,如果你运气不好,它会把我们所有人都变成回形针;而是像其他每一次计算机科学的突破一样,你能够实现一些令人印象深刻的东西,然后你就得想点别的办法。

speaker: Unknown
en: Which brings us to the something else.
zh: 这就把我们带到了那个「别的办法」。

speaker: Unknown
en: And you've already actually used a few phrases that I like here.
zh: 而且你其实已经用了几个我很喜欢的说法。

speaker: Unknown
en: Buzzword compliance is a great one.
zh: 流行词合规就是一个很棒的。

speaker: Unknown
en: And in the book, Reverse Centaur's Guide to Life After AI, I kind of want to walk through it in terms of some of the fun phrases you brought up.
zh: 在《反向半人马:AI 之后生活指南》这本书里,我有点想围绕你提出的那些有趣的短语来展开讲讲。

speaker: Unknown
en: So let's start with reverse centaur.
zh: 那我们从反向半人马开始。

speaker: Unknown
en: What is a reverse centaur compared to a centaur?
zh: 反向半人马和半人马相比是什么?

speaker: Unknown
en: And how does that apply to AI?
zh: 这又如何应用到 AI 上?

speaker: Unknown
en: Well, this is not the first time that labor and capital have come into conflict over automation.
zh: 嗯,这不是劳工和资本第一次因自动化发生冲突了。

speaker: Unknown
en: There's actually a pretty rich literature.
zh: 实际上有相当丰富的文献。

speaker: Unknown
en: One of the truisms of that literature is that when labor drives uptake of automation, it is typically in service to improving the quality of the outputs.
zh: 那些文献的一个共识是:当劳工推动自动化的采用时,通常是为了提升产出的质量。

speaker: Unknown
en: Workers just think they can do cool and amazing things.
zh: 工人们只是觉得他们能做出很酷很了不起的东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: If you go back to the web bubble and you read the business press, it's full of articles going, what are CEOs going to do with all these young workers who've used the web at university who expect to find it in the workplace?
zh: 如果你回到 web 泡沫时期去读商业媒体,里面满是这类文章:CEO 们要拿这些在大学里用过 web、期望在工作场所也能用到 web 的年轻员工怎么办?

speaker: Unknown
en: They're not equipped.
zh: 他们没有准备好。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's the opposite of the articles we have now, which brings me to what happens when you have capital-driven automation, right?
zh: 这与我们现有的文章相反，这就引出了一个问题：当你拥有资本驱动的自动化时，会发生什么，对吧？

speaker: Unknown
en: When you have capital-driven automation, it's typically in service to increasing throughput, often at the expense of quality and worker wellbeing.
zh: 当你拥有资本驱动的自动化时，它通常是为了提高吞吐量，往往以牺牲质量和员工福祉为代价。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so this is particularly valuable when you have a cartelized or monopolized market where you can produce inferior outputs without seeing a loss in sales.
zh: 因此，当你面对一个被卡特尔化或垄断化的市场时，这尤其有价值——在那里你可以生产劣质的产出，而不会看到销量下滑。

speaker: Unknown
en: This is more or less what the thesis of inshittification is, that in a world in which competition has been sidelined, regulators have been captured, workers have been tamed, and new market entry through interoperability has been made illegal by the expansion of IP laws, companies can make worse things and still keep their customers.
zh: 这差不多就是“en-shittification”这个论题的核心：在一个竞争被排挤、监管者被收买、工人被驯服、而通过互操作性进入新市场被知识产权法的扩张定为非法的世界里，公司可以把东西做得更糟，却仍然留住客户。

speaker: Unknown
en: They are the only game in town, and no one's going to punish them through non-market means, and so they can just inshittify stuff, which I think we've all felt very sharply.
zh: 它们是镇上唯一的游戏，没有人会通过非市场手段惩罚它们，所以它们可以把东西 en-shittify，我想我们都非常切身地体会过这一点。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so in the world of capital-driven automation, you see increase in throughput, often at the expense of quality, often at the expense of worker well-being.
zh: 因此，在资本驱动的自动化的世界里，你会看到吞吐量增加，往往以牺牲质量为代价，往往以牺牲员工福祉为代价。

speaker: Unknown
en: And that's why today when you pick up the same business press, it's full of articles about how are CEOs gonna convince these workers who think AI is bullshit that they should be using AI on the job, really the opposite of the web era.
zh: 这就是为什么今天当你翻开同样的商业媒体时，上面满是这样的文章：CEO 们要如何说服这些认为 AI 是胡扯的员工，让他们应该在工作中使用 AI——这真的与网络时代完全相反。

speaker: Unknown
en: So this brings us to centaurs and reverse centaurs.
zh: 这就把我们带到了半人马和反向半人马。

en: You know, there's this joke about economists that if an economist sees a $20 bill on the ground, they won't pick it up because if it was really there, someone would have already picked it up because, you know, as we say in economics, there's no such thing as a free lunch.
zh: 你知道,有个关于经济学家的笑话:如果一个经济学家看到地上有张 20 美元的钞票,他不会去捡,因为如果它真的在那儿,早就有人捡走了,因为,你知道,正如我们在经济学中所说,天下没有免费的午餐。

zh: 而认真对待这些事情、尤其是像我这样在其中工作了很长时间的人,

speaker: Unknown

en: And so now we are in this circumstance where supply is caught up with demand, where firms are willing to produce lower quality outputs and endure more downtime and defects in their code because they think that their customers won't mind as much.
zh: 而现在我们处于这样的境地:供应追上了需求,公司愿意产出质量更低的成果,忍受更多的宕机和代码缺陷,因为他们认为客户不会那么在意。

speaker: Unknown
en: So this is in shitification.
zh: 所以这是"劣化"(shitification)。

speaker: Unknown
en: At the code level and not just at the service delivery level.
zh: 发生在代码层面,而不仅仅是在服务交付层面。

speaker: Unknown
en: You see this in system-wide outages in AWS and lots of other platforms that are theoretically too big to fail and supposed to be run like utilities and instead are being run like startups in terms of the SRE commitments.
zh: 你可以在 AWS 和许多其他平台的系统性宕机中看到这一点，这些平台理论上大到不能倒，本应像公用事业一样运营，但在 SRE 承诺方面却像初创公司一样运营。

speaker: Unknown

zh: 所以这意味着，在行业内经历了五十万次裁员之后，现在工厂门口还有其他十个工人，如果你辞职他们就会接替你的工作，这很难。

zh: 而你说科技工人不像音乐家那样处于能组建工会的位置。

speaker: Unknown
en: Musicians unionized because they were brutally exploited and they fought for a union.
zh: 音乐家组建工会是因为他们被残酷剥削，他们为工会而斗争。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I tell you what, if you look at how your boss treats the workers who aren't in high demand,
zh: 而我告诉你，如果你看看你的老板如何对待那些不是高需求的工人，

speaker: Unknown
en: Not an Amazon programmer, but an Amazon warehouse worker who's injured at three times the rate of any other warehouse worker.
zh: 不是亚马逊的程序员，而是亚马逊的仓库工人，他们受伤的比率是任何其他仓库工人的三倍。

speaker: Unknown
en: Not an Apple programmer, but someone assembling an iPhone in China who works in a factory that has a suicide net around it.
zh: 不是苹果的程序员，而是在中国组装 iPhone 的人，他工作的工厂周围有防自杀网。

speaker: Unknown
en: Not someone who programs AI, but someone in Kenya who does the AI data cleaning and who ends up with lifelong psychological trauma because of the tagging they're supposed to be doing of extreme and gore content.
zh: 不是编写 AI 的人，而是在肯尼亚做 AI 数据清洗的人，因为要对极端和血腥内容做标注，最终落下了终身的心理创伤。

speaker: Unknown
en: You can see what your bosses would do to you if they could.
zh: 你就能看到，如果他们能这么做，你的老板会对你做什么。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so if you wanted to get there, I wouldn't start from here, but here's where you are.
zh: 所以如果你想达到那个目标，我不会从这里开始，但这就是你所处的位置。

speaker: Unknown
en: And there is the Tech Workers Coalition.
zh: 有 Tech Workers Coalition(科技工人联盟)。

speaker: Unknown
en: There's tech solidarity.
zh: 有 tech solidarity。

speaker: Unknown
en: At EFF, we're unionized to the Communications Workers of America.
zh: 在 EFF,我们加入了美国通信工人工会(Communications Workers of America)。

speaker: Unknown
en: There are tech shops that are unionizing and tech shops that are trying to unionize.
zh: 有正在组建工会的科技公司，也有正在尝试组建工会的科技公司。

speaker: Unknown
en: And the bad news is, as you say, it's not a good position in terms of your bargaining strength.
zh: 坏消息是，正如你所说，就你的谈判实力而言，这不是一个好的位置。

speaker: Unknown
en: The good news is
zh: 好消息是

speaker: Unknown

zh: 在活着的记忆中，比任何时候都有更多的美国工人想加入工会。

speaker: Unknown
en: And more Americans support the unionization of their neighbors in their workplaces than at any time in generations.
zh: 比几代人以来的任何时候都有更多的美国人支持他们的邻居在工作场所组建工会。

speaker: Unknown

zh: 而且工会拥有的现金储备比劳工运动历史上任何时候都多。

speaker: Unknown

zh: 而现在他们没有把钱花在组织工作上，而他们应该这么做。

zh: 而我们达到目标的方式之一，就是要求我们作为工人，需要得到那些已经加入工会的同志们的关照，他们不应该把这些现金储备

speaker: Unknown
en: As existing solely to benefit the workers who've already been organized, but to add to the pool of unionized workers.
zh: 视为仅仅为了让已经被组织起来的工人受益而存在，而是用来扩大工会工人的队伍。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so go to TechSolidarity, go to the Tech Workers Coalition, find out how to unionize your shop, start having union conversations, because wishing that there was a way to have a better workplace without unionizing, it's like wishing that we had cryptography that only worked when good guys used it, but that stopped working when bad guys used it to hide child sex abuse material or terrorist plots.
zh: 所以去 TechSolidarity,去 Tech Workers Coalition,了解如何在你的公司组建工会，开始进行工会对话，因为祈愿存在一种不用组建工会就能拥有更好工作场所的方法，就像祈愿我们拥有的密码学只在好人使用时有效，而在坏人用它来隐藏儿童性虐待材料或恐怖主义阴谋时就失效。

speaker: Unknown
en: Wanting it badly is not enough.
zh: 强烈的愿望是不够的。

speaker: Unknown
en: There is one reliable, durable mechanism for workers acquiring power in history, and it's solidarity.
zh: 在历史上，只有一种可靠的、持久的机制能让工人获得权力，那就是团结。

speaker: Unknown
en: That's it.
zh: 就是这个。

speaker: Unknown
en: Solidarity.
zh: 团结。

en: It's interesting you bring up the crypto aspect as you do reference this in the book as well, that that's actually what the Clinton administration had tried to do.
zh: 你提到密码学这个方面很有意思，你在书里也引用了这一点，那实际上正是克林顿政府曾试图做的事情。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah.
zh: 是的。

speaker: Unknown
en: To position it as a musician and that only the good guys would use it.
zh: 把它定位成音乐家那样，只有好人会使用它。

en: And that doesn't happen.

en: That's not how that works.
zh: 事情不是那样运作的。

en: Yeah.

zh: 而且不只是他们。

en: Some of those goals I think are legitimate.

zh: 我认为儿童性虐待材料，打击它显然是极其正当的。

en: I don't think you get there by banning working encryption.
zh: 但我不认为通过禁用有效的加密能达到这个目的。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I think the collateral damage from trying
zh: 而且我认为这样尝试造成的附带损害

speaker: Unknown
en: is catastrophic.
zh: 是灾难性的。

speaker: Unknown
en: As we say at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, wanting it badly is not enough.
zh: 正如我们在电子前哨基金会(Electronic Frontier Foundation)所说，强烈的愿望是不够的。

speaker: Unknown
en: So similar question for this area then.
zh: 那么对这个领域也问一个类似的问题。

speaker: Unknown
en: You've given us advice on solidarity, perhaps even unionization.
zh: 你给了我们关于团结、甚至组建工会的建议。

en: How would you advise folks trying to work on what is the right and wrong way to do encryption and data protection?
zh: 对于那些想做加密和数据保护方面正确之事的人，你会给出什么建议？

speaker: Unknown
en: Oh my goodness.
zh: 哦天哪。

en: Well, I would fall back to my work on inshittification here and say that while individuals and startups, they can employ best practices.
zh: 好吧，我会回到我在 inshittification(屎化)方面的工作，说虽然个人和初创公司，他们可以采用最佳实践。

speaker: Unknown
en: I mean, we look at say Signal, right?
zh: 我是说，我们看看比如 Signal,对吧？

speaker: Unknown
en: Which are, who are doing data protection very well.
zh: 他们，他们在数据保护方面做得非常好。

speaker: Unknown
en: They have practiced extreme data minimization.
zh: 他们实践了极致的数据最小化。

speaker: Unknown
en: They have
zh: 他们有

speaker: Unknown
en: forward-looking programs to do quantum-resistant encryption.
zh: 前瞻性的项目来做抗量子加密。

speaker: Unknown
en: They are involved in policy fights and completely uncompromising in their willingness to backdoor the system.
zh: 他们参与政策斗争，并且在给系统留后门这件事上完全毫不妥协地反对。

speaker: Unknown
en: They are also working very rigorously to highlight
zh: 他们也在非常严谨地致力于强调

speaker: Unknown
en: The fact that prohibitions on jailbreaking phones makes them vulnerable because if Apple and Google say that they won't carry them unless they backdoor their encryption, then the majority of their users are going to lose it.

speaker: Unknown
en: So they're really fighting the whole policy fight, as well as making best of breed, open, inspectable technology.
zh: 所以他们真的在整个政策战线上作战，同时也打造最好的、开放的、可检查的技术。

speaker: Unknown
en: You know, your security technology has to be open and inspectable because there's no security in obscurity.
zh: 你知道，你的安全技术必须是开放且可检查的，因为隐蔽中不存在安全。

speaker: Unknown
en: And as Bruce Schneier says, anyone can devise a security system that works so well that they themselves can't think of a way of breaking it.
zh: 正如 Bruce Schneier 所说，任何人都能设计出一个好到自己都想不出破解办法的安全系统。

speaker: Unknown
en: It doesn't mean that it works.
zh: 但这不意味着它真的有效。

speaker: Unknown
en: It just means it works on people stupider than you.
zh: 只意味着它对比你笨的人有效。

speaker: Unknown
en: So all of that being said, right, none of that stuff is rocket surgery.
zh: 说了这么多，对吧，这些事情没有一件是火箭科学。

speaker: Unknown
en: Like we have companies that have been doing this forever.
zh: 我们有公司做这些事已经很久了。

speaker: Unknown
en: We know what best practices look like.
zh: 我们知道最佳实践长什么样。

en: This raises this question, why don't we have more best practices?

en: And the answer is that we have an enchitogenic policy environment.

en: We have an environment where if two companies decide no one should have end-to-end encryption, no one gets it.
zh: 我们所处的环境是，如果两家公司决定任何人不该有端到端加密，那就没有人能得到它。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so far, that's been good in the West.
zh: 到目前为止，这在西方还算好的。

speaker: Unknown
en: But in China, Apple turned off all the working encryption tools for its iOS platform.

en: And because that platform's locked down and it's illegal to reverse engineer, that's what the Chinese get.

speaker: Unknown
en: All their cloud storage has got a backdoor.

en: The encryption on the wire also has deliberately introduced defects.

en: So you have this place where

en: One person gets to decide whether or not billions of people have privacy and security, whether their governments can find out who the dissidents are, round them up and put them in a camp, which is a thing that Americans need to worry about now as well.

speaker: Unknown
en: And so in an environment where...
zh: 所以在这样的环境里……

speaker: Unknown

zh: 而 Seth,他参与过很多大型开源项目，在其中他进行深入思考等等。

zh: 最终——而我不能告诉你是他写的，因为他没有披露自己写了它，因为从技术上讲，写这首诗是重罪，而这正是他的全部观点，即政府已经把创作文学作品变成了重罪，而这是对第一修正案的表面上的违反。

speaker: Unknown

zh: 去查一查。

zh: 太棒了。

zh: 所以写代码是很了不起的，但它不是软件工程。

zh: 至于软件工程，CACM(ACM 通讯)刚发表了一篇非常好的文章，研究了软件工程师工作中写代码所占的比例。

zh: 不是主要且重要的部分。

zh: 所以 LLM 让你能更快地完成工作的一部分，但它们不能让你更快地完成工作的其余部分。

zh: 有一个众所周知的、叫做自动化盲视的问题，就是说当一台机器通常运行正确，而你本应对极少数它运行出错的罕见情况保持警惕时——

speaker: Unknown
en: Wrong when you're supposed to be the human in the loop.
zh: 出错的那些时候，当你本应是那个在环中的人类时——

speaker: Unknown
en: You can't maintain vigilance.

zh: 人类的神经系统似乎无法对只偶尔发生的事情保持警觉，这就是为什么我们创造了 TSA 里那些人类有史以来最会找水瓶的家伙，然而他们 95% 的时间里都无法发现红队带过 X 光机的假枪。

speaker: Unknown
en: Right.
zh: 对。

zh: 因为他们无法对这些从未发生过的事情保持警觉。

en: So if your programmer using AI to write code in a way that does not require superhuman vigilance, you know, an example might be in radiology, the difference between a radiologist who examines x-rays and gets a second opinion from the AI when the AI disagrees and says, check that x-ray again.
zh: 所以，如果你是程序员，用 AI 写代码的方式不应要求超人的警觉性。你知道，一个例子可能是在放射学中，一边是检查 X 光片、并在 AI 不同意并说“再检查一下那张 X 光片”时听取 AI 第二意见的放射科医生。

speaker: Unknown
en: Which is a thing where you're just doing your job but at a higher degree of fidelity that stops people from dying of cancer versus the radiologist who sees nine-tenths of their colleagues fired and who then has to review a hundred times as many x-rays that the AI has vetted and says are cancer free and they have to make sure that the AI is right and if the AI is wrong three percent of the time they're probably going to miss all of it and then people are going to die and you know that's not what the machine does that's who it does it for and who it does it to that's the social arrangement of the machine not the technical capabilities of it.
zh: 在这种情况下，你只是在做自己的工作，但保真度更高，能防止人们死于癌症；另一边则是那个看到十分之九的同事被裁掉的放射科医生，他随后必须审查是原来一百倍之多的、AI 已审核并判定无癌的 X 光片，他必须确保 AI 是对的，而如果 AI 有 3% 的出错率，他很可能会漏掉全部错误，然后人们就会死去。你知道，这不是机器做的事，而是它为谁做、对谁做——这是机器的社会性安排，而不是它的技术能力。

speaker: Unknown
en: To me, that was probably the most impactful example of a reverse centaur versus a centaur itself.
zh: 对我来说，那可能是半人马反面与半人马本身相比最有冲击力的例子。

speaker: Unknown
en: But first, I have to ask, for the sake of the technical users, there are a lot of people who are trying to protest models or AIs as created today in terms of free speech.
zh: 但首先，为了技术用户，我必须问一下，现在有很多人试图以言论自由的名义为如今的模型或 AI 进行抗辩。

speaker: Unknown
en: And you're a notable free speech advocate, and you mentioned this.
zh: 而你是一位著名的言论自由倡导者，你也提到了这一点。

en: Can you walk us through how is it that free speech laws protect things like the DECSS haiku and model generation for AIs?
zh: 你能带我们梳理一下，言论自由法律是如何保护诸如 DECSS 俳句和 AI 的模型生成之类的东西的？

speaker: Unknown
en: So in the 90s...
zh: 所以在 90 年代……

speaker: Unknown
en: The NSA had classed, as you said, classed working encryption as ammunition.
zh: NSA 曾把——如你所说——把可用的加密技术归类为弹药。

speaker: Unknown
en: And EFF and our fellow fighters for working encryption, privacy, and security raised a lot of arguments about why this was bad.
zh: 而 EFF 和我们那些为可用加密、隐私与安全而战的同伴们提出了很多论据，说明为什么这是糟糕的。

speaker: Unknown
en: The NSA said, all of this parade of horribles you proposed that will happen if we don't have working encryption, they're just hysterics.
zh: NSA 说，你们提出的这一连串如果不使用可用加密就会发生的可怕情景，都只是歇斯底里。

speaker: Unknown
en: We will let you use a cipher called DES50, Defense Encryption Standard of 50 Bits.
zh: 我们会允许你们使用一种叫做 DES50 的密码，即 50 位国防加密标准。

speaker: Unknown
en: That is so secure that no bad guy will ever break it, but not so secure that we can't break it.
zh: 它安全到没有坏人能破解它，但又没有安全到我们破解不了它。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so we'll catch all the bad guys.
zh: 这样我们就能抓住所有坏人。

speaker: Unknown
en: And we made a lot of arguments about the technical insufficiency of DES50.
zh: 而我们就 DES50 在技术上的不足提出了很多论据。

speaker: Unknown
en: No one really cared.
zh: 没有人真正在意。

speaker: Unknown
en: The NSA had hired like the largest plurality of top mathematicians from all the IVs and Big Ten schools for 50 years.
zh: NSA 在 50 年里雇用了来自所有常春藤盟校和十大联盟学校中占比最大的顶尖数学家。

speaker: Unknown
en: And people were like, whoa, whoa, whoa.
zh: 而人们就像：哇，哇，哇。

speaker: Unknown
en: Who are you to say that this doesn't work?
zh: 你凭什么说这行不通？

en: So then we proved it.
zh: 于是我们就证明了它。

speaker: Unknown

speaker: Unknown
en: And also the Usenet alt hierarchy is quite a storied technologist.
zh: 还有 Usenet 的 alt 层级也是他建的，他是一位颇有传奇色彩的技术专家。

speaker: Unknown
en: John built a computer.
zh: John 造了一台计算机。

speaker: Unknown
en: He made some custom ASICs.
zh: 他做了一些定制 ASIC。

speaker: Unknown

zh: 那台计算机叫 Deepcrack。

speaker: Unknown
en: It cost a quarter million dollars and it could brute force all of DES50 in two and a half hours.
zh: 它花了 25 万美元，能够在两个半小时内暴力破解全部 DES50。

speaker: Unknown
en: We brought that into Quora.
zh: 我们把它带到了 Quora。

speaker: Unknown
en: We brought that into Congress and we said, look, if the mafia is willing to spend a quarter of a million dollars,
zh: 我们把它带到国会，并说，听着，如果黑手党愿意花 25 万美元，

speaker: Unknown
en: They're going to be able to decrypt all the financial transactions in America, all the corporate secrets, all the individual information.
zh: 他们就能解密美国所有的金融交易、所有的企业机密、所有的个人信息。

speaker: Unknown
en: Someday when we're pushing firmware updates to anti-lock breaking systems or people's pacemakers, that will be an open book to griefers and foreign spies and what have you.
zh: 将来有一天，当我们向防抱死刹车系统或人们的心脏起搏器推送固件更新时，这些都会对恶意破坏者、外国间谍之类的人完全敞开。

speaker: Unknown
en: And again, they were like, yeah, that sounds stupid.
zh: 结果他们还是说， yeah,那听起来很蠢。

speaker: Unknown
en: Go away.
zh: 走开。

speaker: Unknown
en: So then we brought the lawyers in.
zh: 于是我们把律师请了进来。

speaker: Unknown
en: And Cindy Cohen, my former boss, has just retired from EFF and has written a wonderful memoir of this period.
zh: Cindy Cohen,我以前的老板，刚从 EFF 退休，并就这段时期写了一本精彩的回忆录。

speaker: Unknown
en: Cindy Cohen, called Privacy's Defender, I should say, Cindy Cohen formulated a radical argument.
zh: 名叫《Privacy's Defender》。应该说，是 Cindy Cohen 提出了一个激进的主张。

speaker: Unknown
en: She said the First Amendment protects expressive speech and code is a form of expressive speech.
zh: 她说，第一修正案保护表达性言论，而代码是表达性言论的一种形式。

speaker: Unknown
en: And a lot of people at the time were like, I don't get it.
zh: 当时很多人都说，我不明白。

speaker: Unknown
en: How can code be expressive speech?
zh: 代码怎么能是表达性言论呢？

speaker: Unknown
en: But we represented a programmer called Daniel J. Bernstein.
zh: 但我们代理了一位叫 Daniel J. Bernstein 的程序员。

speaker: Unknown
en: He was a graduate student at UC Berkeley, and he was publishing the source for a cipher that was stronger than DES50 and therefore ammunition on Usenet, this early messaging system that predated the web.
zh: 他当时是 UC Berkeley 的研究生，正在发布一种比 DES50 更强的密码的源代码，因此在 Usenet 上——这个早于万维网的早期消息系统——算是弹药。

speaker: Unknown
en: And we went to court on his behalf and the judge agreed with us that this math that he was producing, this code he was producing was a form of expressive speech and that the First Amendment protected it.
zh: 我们代表他走上法庭，法官同意了我们的观点：他产出的这些数学、他产出的这些代码是一种表达性言论，受第一修正案保护。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then we went to the appellate division and the appellate division agreed and the NSA did not want to try their chances at the Supreme Court.
zh: 然后我们上诉到上诉法院，上诉法院也同意了，而 NSA 不想在最高法院碰运气。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so since about 1993, it has been legal to have encryption that works.
zh: 所以从大约 1993 年起，拥有真正能用的加密就是合法的。

speaker: Unknown
en: And this is how we protect everything.
zh: 而这就是我们保护一切的方式。

speaker: Unknown
en: I mean, everything.
zh: 我是说，一切。

speaker: Unknown
en: And it's because of this free speech tradition.
zh: 而这是拜这一言论自由传统所赐。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so when people say that we should ban certain code with a kind of scrutiny, so there's some speech that's unlawful, obviously.
zh: 所以当人们说我们应该以某种审查标准禁止某些代码时——当然，有些言论是非法的。

speaker: Unknown
en: But the constitutionality of a law that bans certain speech is very fraught and requires that the ban be very narrowly construed and fall into a very small number of purposes and that the speech itself
zh: 但禁止某些言论的法律，其合宪性是非常微妙的问题，要求禁令必须被解释得非常狭窄，落入非常少数的用途范围，并且该言论本身

speaker: Unknown
en: be of a low degree of democratic importance.
zh: 民主重要性程度要低。

speaker: Unknown
en: So restrictions on political speech, for example, are very hard to craft in a way that comports with the Constitution, because one of the purposes of the First Amendment is to guarantee political discourse.
zh: 比如对政治言论的限制，就很难以符合宪法的方式来制定，因为第一修正案的用途之一就是保障政治讨论。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so this is one of the reasons that most so-called political disinformation and misinformation is probably illegal.
zh: 这也是为什么大多数所谓的政治虚假信息和错误信息很可能是合法的原因之一。

speaker: Unknown
en: Not all of it.
zh: 不是全部。

speaker: Unknown
en: I mean, stuff like vote next Wednesday when the vote is on Tuesday is illegal.
zh: 我是说，比如投票是周二却让人「下周三去投票」这种事是非法的。

speaker: Unknown
en: Fraud, like deceiving people is illegal, but like having a thing labeled as a deepfake, right?
zh: 欺诈，比如欺骗他人，是非法的，但比如把一个东西标注为深度伪造，对吧？

speaker: Unknown
en: Where you're like, we're about to show you a deepfake of politician X saying some things that are a paraphrase of what we think he would do is legal.
zh: 就是那种说「我们即将展示政客 X 的深度伪造视频，他说的话是我们对他可能会做什么的改述」——这是合法的。

speaker: Unknown
en: Because the First Amendment protects it, because the First Amendment is very, very delicate about restricting political speech.
zh: 因为第一修正案保护它，因为第一修正案对限制政治言论这件事非常、非常谨慎。

speaker: Unknown
en: And one of the things that we're seeing right now is what happens when a government decides that it is not interested in protecting dissident political speech.
zh: 而我们现在正在目睹的事情之一就是，当一个政府决定它无意保护持不同政见者的政治言论时，会发生什么。

speaker: Unknown
en: And how dangerous and frightening that is to the democratic project.
zh: 以及这对民主事业是多么危险和可怕。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so there are outputs of AIs that are unlawful speech, but I would be reluctant to say that we should lower the degree of scrutiny we apply to restrictions on code itself, including code that embodies a model.
zh: 所以确实存在 AI 的输出属于非法言论的情况，但我不愿意说我们应该降低对代码本身之限制所适用的审查严格程度，包括承载了模型的代码。

speaker: Unknown
en: Not least because it's very hard to make that restriction stick.
zh: 尤其是因为这种限制很难真正落地。

speaker: Unknown
en: What are you going to do?
zh: 你打算怎么做？

speaker: Unknown
en: Make every Git server in the world comply with orders to take down the code that embodies the model?
zh: 让世界上每一个 Git 服务器都遵守下架承载模型的代码的命令吗？

speaker: Unknown
en: How is that going to work?
zh: 那要怎么运作？

speaker: Unknown
en: It doesn't seem practical.
zh: 看起来不现实。

speaker: Unknown
en: I really wish we could spend more time talking about what goes into this.
zh: 我真希望我们能花更多时间聊聊这里面的门道。

speaker: Unknown
en: You also have content in the book about scraping and how that can be very, very good.
zh: 书里还有关于爬取的内容，以及它如何可以非常、非常好。

speaker: Unknown
en: But we do have to move towards the end of the interview.
zh: 但我们确实得接近访谈的尾声了。

speaker: Unknown
en: So let's talk about what comes next.
zh: 那么我们来谈谈接下来会怎样。

speaker: Unknown
en: What is dogshit unit economics in AI and what do you think comes after a bubble burst or perhaps even why is the bubble going to burst?
zh: 什么是 AI 中糟糕的单位经济学,以及你认为泡沫破裂之后会发生什么,或者说泡沫究竟为什么会破裂?

speaker: Unknown
en: So AI has bad economics and it has bad unit economics too.
zh: 所以 AI 的经济性很差,它的单位经济学也很差。

speaker: Unknown
en: So unit economics, that's how a business performs when it moves another unit, right?
zh: 单位经济学,指的是一项业务在多做一个单位时的表现,对吧?

speaker: Unknown
en: When it makes a sale or acquires a customer.
zh: 比如完成一笔销售,或者获取一个客户。

speaker: Unknown
en: So like what happens at the margin?
zh: 也就是在边际上发生了什么?

speaker: Unknown
en: So the web lost money early on and AI is losing money.
zh: 早期 Web 是亏钱的,而 AI 也在亏钱。

speaker: Unknown
en: And some people who say that AI has got a path to profitability use the fact that the web lost money as proof that AI will make money someday.
zh: 一些说 AI 有盈利之路的人,拿 Web 曾经过赔钱这件事当作证据,证明 AI 终有一天会赚钱。

speaker: Unknown
en: But for that to be like a valid logical construct, it would have to be the case that losing money was itself a predictor of making money.
zh: → [[572]] 唯一盈利的那家公司是 NVIDIA。

speaker: Unknown
en: And broadly, losing money is a predictor of losing more money.
zh: 而总体来看,亏钱是亏更多钱的预测因子。

speaker: Unknown
en: And the exceptions to that have to have a set of criteria, have to satisfy a set of criteria that are themselves not a guarantee but at least increase the likelihood.
zh: 而那些例外必须满足一套标准,必须满足一套标准,这套标准本身虽然不是保证,但至少能提高可能性:

speaker: Unknown
en: That you're going to go from a money losing cash basis to a money winning profitable basis.
zh: 让你从亏现金的赔钱基础,转变为赚钱的盈利基础。

speaker: Unknown
en: And first among those characteristics is good unit economics.
zh: 而这些特征中排在第一位的就是良好的单位经济学。

speaker: Unknown
en: So every new web user, even in its money losing his days, made the web more profitable as a sector.
zh: 所以每一个新的 Web 用户,即便在它赔钱的日子里,都让 Web 作为一个行业变得更赚钱。

speaker: Unknown
en: Every visit to the web by a web user made the web as a sector more profitable.
zh: Web 用户的每一次访问,都让 Web 作为一个行业更赚钱。

speaker: Unknown
en: And every generation of web technology was more profitable than the previous generation.
zh: 而每一代 Web 技术都比上一代更赚钱。

speaker: Unknown
en: This is very different from AI.
zh: 这与 AI 截然不同。

speaker: Unknown
en: Every AI user that an AI company acquires knocks another hole in their balance sheet.
zh: AI 公司每获取一个 AI 用户,都在它们的资产负债表上又砸出一个洞。

speaker: Unknown
en: Every time that user comes back, the balance sheet bleeds more red ink.
zh: 那个用户每回来一次,资产负债表上就多流一分红字。

speaker: Unknown
en: Every generation of AI loses more money than the previous generation of AI.
zh: AI 的每一代都比上一代亏更多的钱。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's the money-losingest thing we've ever done.
zh: 这是我们有史以来亏钱亏得最狠的东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: And we're losing a lot of money to it.
zh: 而且我们正在为它亏掉大量的钱。

speaker: Unknown
en: Seven companies make up 35% of the S&P 500, the so-called Magnificent Seven, and six of them are losing hundreds of billions of dollars.
zh: 七家公司构成了标普 500 指数的 35%,即所谓的「七巨头」,其中六家正在亏损数千亿美元。

speaker: Unknown
en: The company that is profitable is NVIDIA.
zh: 赚钱的那家公司是 NVIDIA。

speaker: Unknown
en: That's the company that's getting the hundreds of billions of dollars and then loaning it to those six other companies so they can buy more of NVIDIA's products.
zh: 就是那家拿到数千亿美元、然后再把钱借给那六家公司,好让它们去买更多 NVIDIA 产品的公司。

speaker: Unknown
en: From NVIDIA, this is not good.
zh: 买的还是 NVIDIA 自己的产品,这可不妙。

speaker: Unknown
en: The sector is not making anywhere near what it's spending and it's spending more, but its earnings are not coming up.
zh: 这个行业赚的钱远远比不上它的支出,而且它支出越来越多,收益却没有涨上来。

speaker: Unknown
en: You may have seen Anthropic argue that it was profitable, but if you look closely at that announcement, what you'll find is that Anthropic is only profitable
zh: 你可能见过 Anthropic 声称自己已经盈利,但如果你仔细看那份声明,你会发现 Anthropic 只在一种情况下盈利:

speaker: Unknown
en: If you ignore the generally accepted accounting practices, GAAP, the gold standard for figuring out whether a business is profitable.
zh: 那就是忽略公认会计准则(GAAP)——判断一家企业是否盈利的黄金标准。

speaker: Unknown
en: So fundamentally what they've said is we're profitable in such a cool way you can't express it with normal math.
zh: 所以本质上它们说的是:我们以一种非常酷的方式盈利,以至于你无法用正常的数学来表达它。

speaker: Unknown
en: And they can't tell us which math they're profitable by, just that there is a math under which they're profitable.
zh: 而且它们没法告诉我们是按哪种数学它们才盈利的,只说存在某种数学,按那种数学它们是盈利的。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's a little like their announcement about Mythos, which is like, we're about to have an IPO, and we've invented a security auditing tool that's so powerful that you're not allowed to see it.
zh: 这有点像它们关于 Mythos 的声明,大意是:我们马上要 IPO 了,而且我们发明了一个强大到不允许你们看到的安全审计工具。

speaker: Unknown
en: Did we mention we're about to have an IPO?
zh: 我们提到过我们马上要 IPO 了吗?

speaker: Unknown
en: And I just think we have a thing that's really valuable that we'd like you to buy, but we're not gonna show it to you because it's so cool.
zh: → [[586]] 一个东西不是真的,不代表它没有用。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's not an argument that should persuade people.
zh: 这不是一个应该能说服人的论点。

speaker: Unknown
en: That's a monumentally unpersuasive argument.
zh: 这是一个毫无说服力到堪称纪念碑式的论点。

speaker: Unknown
en: And it may be that it does good things, right?
zh: 当然,它也许真能带来好东西,对吧?

speaker: Unknown
en: It needn't be useless to not be true.
zh: 不真实未必就没有用。

speaker: Unknown
en: You could invent a security auditing tool that will perform a $20,000 security audit using $50,000 worth of tokens.
zh: 你可以发明一个安全审计工具,用价值 5 万美元的 token 完成一次价值 2 万美元的安全审计。

speaker: Unknown
en: And that would be an impressive computer science feat and a way to go broke.
zh: 那会是一项令人印象深刻的计算机科学壮举,同时也是一种破产的方式。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so without being able to look at it, we can't make any claims about it and we should apply a skeptical lens.
zh: 所以在没法看到它的情况下,我们无法对它做出任何断言,我们应该戴上怀疑的镜片。

speaker: Unknown
en: The economics get worse when you look at the claims about inference.
zh: 当你去看关于推理的那些说法时,经济性变得更糟了。

speaker: Unknown
en: If they can do what, say, the railroad companies do, which is like you put a lot of money into capital, you put down the rails, and you buy the rail cars, and then your operating expenses are really low.
zh: 如果它们能做到比如说铁路公司做的事,那就是:投入大量资金到资本上,铺下铁轨,买下火车车厢,然后你的运营费用就非常低。

speaker: Unknown
en: So even though you had a giant CapEx, you can make it back.
zh: 这样即便你有一笔巨额资本支出(CapEx),你也能把它赚回来。

speaker: Unknown
en: Or if you go bankrupt, then the people who buy your hard assets at a bankruptcy can make it back, operating those assets and amortizing them out over a long duty cycle.
zh: 或者如果你破产了,那些在破产中买下你的硬资产的人可以把它赚回来,通过运营这些资产并在一个漫长的使用周期里把它们摊销掉。

speaker: Unknown
en: They keep claiming that their inference costs are coming down.
zh: 它们一直声称它们的推理成本在下降。

speaker: Unknown
en: When we look at their actual internal figures, that's not in evidence.
zh: 但当我们看它们实际的内部数据时,证据并不支持这一点。

speaker: Unknown
en: So Ed Zitron is a very good AI finance and tech critic, got a hold of a balance sheet from OpenAI, their finances from OpenAI.
zh: Ed Zitron 是一位非常优秀的 AI 金融与科技批评家,他拿到了一份来自 OpenAI 的资产负债表,OpenAI 的财务数据。

speaker: Unknown
en: And what he saw was that it's true that they are on the line item for inference, it's really low.
zh: 他看到的是,在「推理」这个科目上,数字确实很低,这是真的。

speaker: Unknown
en: But if you keep reading down the balance sheet to the line item for marketing, what you find is they claim they're spending as much on marketing as Coca-Cola.
zh: 但如果你继续往下读资产负债表,读到「市场营销」这个科目,你会发现它们声称自己在市场营销上的花费和可口可乐一样多。

speaker: Unknown
en: Now, Coca-Cola has three global ad agencies that mostly just service them.
zh: 而可口可乐有三家全球广告公司,基本只服务于它一家。

speaker: Unknown
en: They have billboards everywhere.
zh: 他们的广告牌到处都是。

speaker: Unknown
en: Like, if you want to find out where Coca-Cola's marketing budget has gone, you can just count noses in the ad agencies and count billboards by the side of the highway, right?
zh: 比如，如果你想知道可口可乐的营销预算花到哪儿去了，你只需要数一数广告公司里的人数，再数一数高速公路边的广告牌，对吧？

speaker: Unknown
en: And you can figure out that they're spending that money on marketing.
zh: 然后你就能算出他们把那笔钱花在营销上了。

speaker: Unknown
en: That's not an evidence for OpenAI.
zh: 这对 OpenAI 来说可不是证据。

speaker: Unknown
en: Ed's theory, which I think is true, is that they have taken a bunch of hundred dollar bills and sold them for a dollar each.
zh: Ed 的理论——我认为是对的——是他们拿了一大堆百元大钞，然后每张一块钱卖掉了。

speaker: Unknown
en: By giving people really cheap inference.
zh: 就是通过给人们非常便宜的推理服务。

speaker: Unknown
en: And rather than calling that an inference expense, they're calling it a marketing expense.
zh: 而他们不把这叫推理开支，而是叫营销开支。

speaker: Unknown
en: But even if we take them at their word and say, okay, you've figured out how to make inference cheap, you've got the hard assets, you've done the capital expenditure involved in making the model, you can rest on your laurels.
zh: 但即使我们相信他们的话，说好吧，你们已经想出办法让推理变便宜了，你们手里有硬资产，你们已经完成了构建模型所需的资本支出，你们可以躺在功劳簿上休息了。

speaker: Unknown
en: We can then look at the low switching costs as evidenced by the huge exodus from ChatGPT to Claude when the new Claude model came out that was demonstrably better than ChatGPT.
zh: 那我们就可以看看低转换成本，证据就是当新的 Claude 模型发布、明显比 ChatGPT 更好的时候，用户大规模从 ChatGPT 迁移到 Claude。

speaker: Unknown
en: Which means that OpenAI doesn't get to just make a model and stop.
zh: 这意味着 OpenAI 不能只造一个模型然后停手。

speaker: Unknown
en: They don't have to make another model or they're out of business.
zh: 他们必须再做另一个模型，否则就出局了。

speaker: Unknown
en: And the day they do, Anthropic has to make a successor to Claude.
zh: 而他们这么做的当天，Anthropic 就得做一个 Claude 的后继者。

speaker: Unknown
en: So how do you get these balance sheets right side up?
zh: 那么，你怎么把这些资产负债表扶正呢？

speaker: Unknown
en: How do you take a trillion dollars in expenditure and $50 million in revenue and turn it into a profit?
zh: 你怎么把一万亿的支出和五千万的营收变成利润？

speaker: Unknown
en: How do you do it when your assets need to be replaced every three to five years?
zh: 当你的资产每三到五年就要更换一次时，你怎么做到？

speaker: Unknown
en: How do you do it when your operating expenses are not coming down?
zh: 当你的运营成本降不下来时，你怎么做到？

speaker: Unknown
en: How do you do it when your unit economics suck?
zh: 当你的单位经济模型很糟糕时，你怎么做到？

speaker: Unknown
en: I don't think you do.
zh: 我不认为你能做到。

speaker: Unknown
en: I don't think that business has a future, at least not the way they're running it.
zh: 我不认为这门生意有未来，至少按照他们现在运营的方式没有。

speaker: Unknown
en: I look forward to the sequel to Reverse Centaur describing post-bubble all the open source models.
zh: 我期待《Reverse Centaur》的续集，描述泡沫破灭之后的所有开源模型。

speaker: Unknown
en: I would really love to keep talking with you about this, Corey.
zh: 我很想继续和你聊这个话题，Corey。

speaker: Unknown
en: This is fascinating stuff, but unfortunately, we've reached roughly the end of the book and the end of time.
zh: 这些内容非常精彩，但不幸的是，我们已经差不多到了书的结尾，也是时间的尽头。

speaker: Unknown
en: If you wanted people to find out more about you, your writing, the EFF, where would you direct them on the internet?
zh: 如果你想让人们更多地了解你、你的写作、EFF，你会把他们在互联网上引向哪里？

speaker: Unknown
en: Start at EFF.org, join, be a member.
zh: 从 EFF.org 开始，加入，成为会员。

speaker: Unknown
en: We're a member supported nonprofit, but also sign up for our mailing list, find out what's going on, get involved in your local tech and politics questions, and be a part of the oldest, most important and most effective digital rights group in the world.
zh: 我们是一个由会员支持的非营利组织，另外也请注册我们的邮件列表，了解正在发生的事情，参与你本地的科技和政治议题，成为世界上最古老、最重要、最有效的数字权利组织的一员。

speaker: Unknown
en: To find my stuff, I'm published by Macmillan.
zh: 要找到我的作品，我的出版商是 Macmillan。

speaker: Unknown
en: I've written more than 30 books, science fiction, science fiction for kids, science fiction for teens, picture books, graphic novels, tech policy books, collections of essays, even a little art book of my weird collages.
zh: 我写了三十多本书，科幻小说、儿童科幻、青少年科幻、绘本、图像小说、科技政策书籍、随笔集，甚至还有一本我那些奇怪拼贴画的小小艺术书。

speaker: Unknown
en: And all of them, except for the weird collage book, which was a very limited edition, are for sale anywhere books are sold.
zh: 除了那本限量版的奇怪拼贴书之外，所有这些书在任何卖书的地方都有售。

speaker: Unknown
en: And you can get my eBooks and my audio books anywhere books are sold, except Amazon won't carry my audio books because they're DRM free.
zh: 你可以在任何卖书的地方买到我的电子书和有声书，但 Amazon 不会上架我的有声书，因为它们没有 DRM。

speaker: Unknown
en: So you can get them places that aren't Amazon, including from me directly at craphound.com slash shop.
zh: 所以你可以在不是 Amazon 的地方买到它们，包括直接从我这里，在 craphound.com/shop。

speaker: Unknown
en: DRM free, no user license.
zh: 无 DRM，没有用户许可协议。

speaker: Unknown
en: You bought them, you own them.
zh: 你买了它们，你就拥有它们。

speaker: Unknown
en: Don't violate copyright law, but sell them, give them away, loan them out.
zh: 不要违反版权法，但你可以卖掉它们、送人、借出去。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's fine.
zh: 没问题。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then pluralistic.net is my newsletter.
zh: 然后pluralistic.net是我的通讯。

speaker: Unknown
en: I write four to six essays a week there, and I syndicate it according to the grand tradition of Posse, post own site, share everywhere.
zh: 我在那里每周写四到六篇随笔，并且按照 Posse 的伟大传统进行联合发布：发布在自己的网站上，然后分享到各处。

speaker: Unknown
en: So I turn every one of those essays into a thread on Mastodon, another one on Blue Sky.
zh: 所以我把每篇随笔都变成 Mastodon 上的一个帖子串，还有 Blue Sky 上的另一个。

speaker: Unknown
en: I paste it into Medium and Tumblr.
zh: 我把它粘贴到 Medium 和 Tumblr 上。

speaker: Unknown
en: I'm the last Tumblr user on Earth.
zh: 我是地球上最后一个 Tumblr 用户。

speaker: Unknown
en: I have a old-fashioned mailman list.
zh: 我有一个老式的 mailman 邮件列表。

speaker: Unknown
en: I use mailman because it's open and I use no analytics.
zh: 我用 mailman 因为它是开放的，而且我不使用任何分析工具。

speaker: Unknown
en: I don't even know how many subscribers I have, let alone what my open rate is.
zh: 我甚至不知道我有多少订阅者，更不用说我的打开率是多少了。

speaker: Unknown
en: My website has no tracking.
zh: 我的网站没有任何追踪。

speaker: Unknown
en: My privacy policy is I don't collect any of your information, never will, and never use it in any way.
zh: 我的隐私政策是：我不收集你的任何信息，永远不会，也绝不会以任何方式使用它。

speaker: Unknown
en: And it's Creative Commons Attribution.
zh: 而且它采用 Creative Commons 署名许可。

speaker: Unknown
en: So if you see something there that you like, you can share it, you can give it away, you can sell it, you can translate it, make a video out of it, set it to music, whatever you want to do.
zh: 所以如果你在那里看到喜欢的东西，你可以分享它、送人、卖掉它、翻译它、做成视频、配上音乐，随你想做什么。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's refreshing to hear.
zh: 听到这些真让人耳目一新。

speaker: Unknown
en: Well, all that being said, thank you again, Corey, for coming on to Software Engineering Daily.
zh: 好了，说了这么多，再次感谢你来到 Software Engineering Daily，Corey。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's been lovely to talk to you.
zh: 和你聊天非常愉快。

speaker: Unknown
en: For SED, this is Josh Goldberg.
zh: 代表 SED，我是 Josh Goldberg。

speaker: Unknown
en: Oh, it's been my pleasure.
zh: 哦，这是我的荣幸。

speaker: Unknown
en: Thank you, Josh.
zh: 谢谢你，Josh。

speaker: Unknown
en: Thanks, everyone.
zh: 谢谢大家。

speaker: Unknown
en: Thanks for listening.
zh: 感谢收听。
